items.title: ARTEX Moves at Machine Speed: What Risk Owners Need to Change
items.summary: Key Takeaways ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework released in July 2026, doesn’t exploit new kinds of vulnerabilities. It automates the discovery, chaining, and retrying of existing weaknesses, often across many targets at once. In observed campaigns, attackers using ARTEX went from first targeting an organization to privileged access in under three hours, while the median time for customers to fix critical vulnerabilities is 7 days. In most AI attack tools of this kind, the limits are set by prompts or by user-adjustable settings, so organizations should identify and approve these tools and question any pentest provider that runs them. To keep pace, vulnerability programs need to detect exposures at disclosure, rank them by confirmed exploitability, and make automatic patching the default, with hours-long deadlines for internet-facing systems. ARTEX, an AI-driven penetration-testing framework, didn’t change what gets exploited. It changed how long you have, and how many of your weak points get tried at once. Frameworks like ARTEX don’t need a new class of vulnerability. They automate the work of finding, chaining, and retrying existing weaknesses, often across many targets in parallel. Observed campaigns show that some intrusions reach privileged access within hours. That strengthens the case for faster remediation and mitigation, and for ensuring that a single unpatched system, exposed credential, or excessive permission doesn’t become a much larger intrusion. ARTEX was released as an open-source penetration-testing framework in July 2026. You give it a target and a goal. It scans, picks a way in, uses what it finds there to reach the next system, and keeps going until it reaches the goal or runs out of routes. It was published in July as a research and testing tool. By October, it was turning up in incident reports. For vulnerability and risk management teams, the implication is direct: every hour an exposure remains open gives attackers more time to find and exploit a path through your environment. When they can pursue several paths at once, the question is how quickly you can close the exposures that put critical systems within reach. What ARTEX is We read its source code. The simplest description is a project manager for a break-in. A planning agent takes the goal and keeps an ordered to-do list. The example in ARTEX’s own documentation is the familiar one: find an injection point, take the credentials, move sideways, raise privileges. Worker agents carry out the steps, several at a time, with the same ordinary tools a human tester would use. Each one writes down what it learned, and the planner reads those notes and decides what to try next. A person can watch and redirect it from a web console, and it runs on whichever language model you connect to it. None of that is new to a penetration tester. Scanners have found weaknesses quickly for 20 years. The slow, skilled part of an intrusion was joining those weaknesses into a route, keeping track of what worked, and carrying a stolen credential from one machine to the next, and that is the part ARTEX does. ARTEX did not ship without an authorization-scope mechanism. It shipped with one removed, and the comment saying so is still in the source. The gates that replaced it are seeded as ordinary settings, and a user can disable or delete them. Anatomy of an AI attacker. Seven capabilities taken from the source code of ARTEX, CyberStrikeAI, Hermes, and Cairn, four tools already seen in real attacks. Every layer rests on one weakness you have not fixed yet. What The Reports Say The public evidence comes mainly from Microsoft and CrowdStrike, and it is more measured than the headlines. Microsoft watched one group use ARTEX to attempt sign-ins at more than 2,250 tenants. Most attempts failed, but in several cases the group went from targeting an organization to gaining privileged access in under three hours. CrowdStrike saw another group turn it on more than 200 organizations in 11 days and confirmed follow-on activity at nine, with a human operator steering at the decision points. The agents ran on a cheap, open-weight model, not a premium one. In a separate case, Microsoft timed an agent at 5 minutes from searching GitHub for leaked secrets to pulling data from a cloud key vault. That is the evidence. ARTEX Has Relatives ARTEX has the name, but your team is as likely to meet one of its relatives. We also read the code and documentation for five of them. Tool What it is Used in attacks What keeps it in bounds ARTEX and its forks Runs a full penetration test on its own. The original is closed; the copies are not. Yes By default, lets an action through when its own safety check fails. Cairn Many agents working from one shared board of findings. Yes No controls of its own. In local mode, agents run with your permissions and no sandbox. Hermes General-purpose agent that learns by writing its own skills. Yes Approval for the skills it writes is off by default. CyberStrikeAI Security testing platform with built-in command-and-control, now owned by ThreatBook. Yes Mixed. Unanswered approvals are denied, but tool filtering is a pattern blocklist. Strix Application security agent that aims to prove each finding with a working exploit. Yes Scope is largely set by instructions to the model. PentestGPT Academic project that now runs as an agent. None we found Relies on the isolation you deploy it in. RedAgents / Artex Pro ThreatBook’s commercial bundle, including a paid ARTEX. Not applicable We have not seen the code. The pattern repeats. In most of these tools, the limits are written in prompts, or in settings that someone can change. One platform in the table turns on exactly one rule out of the box: its tool filter blocks government domains, and nothing else. When that rule fires, the message to the agent tells it to pick an authorized non-government target instead. In another case, it goes further. While the agent is writing its reply, a second copy of the conversation runs in the background, writing new skills for it. The approval gate for those writes is off unless you switch it on, and once written, a skill becomes part of its instructions in every session that follows. The tool you approve and the tool that runs next month are not guaranteed to be the same tool. Two Additions to The Asset Inventory The first is everything you forgot. These agents work many targets at once and have no reason to skip the dull ones, so the unowned server gets the same attention as your front door. Gaps in the inventory were tolerable when an attacker had to choose where to spend a week. Now the inventory has to be complete and current, which is what Qualys CyberSecurity Asset Management (CSAM) is built for. The second is the tools themselves. Sooner or later someone in your organization, or at one of your suppliers, will run one of these with good intentions. Each install holds the findings and credentials from every test it has run. One popular mirror’s source was clean, but its installer pulled a Docker image with a backdoor in the login page . The image had been pulled 7,946 times before researchers disclosed it. Treat them like any other software: find them, then approve or remove them. Before your team or your pentest provider runs one Ask five questions, and ask your provider the same ones When a safety check errors out or times out, does the tool stop or carry on? By default, ARTEX carries on. Is scope enforced by the software, or requested in a prompt? What counts as a finding, and what evidence comes with it? Can you show that the build you are running matches source code someone has reviewed? Is every action logged in a way you can tie back to your own test? Seven Da ys Against Three Hours Most vulnerability programs rest on an assumption that rarely gets written down, which is that attackers are short on time. It is why a critical vulnerability on an internet-facing server can be given 30 days, why a privilege escalation bug that needs local access waits behind the remote ones, and why risk exceptions get signed when exploitation looks complicated. ARTEX makes attacker time cheap, and the assumption goes with it. An attacker who can get from first contact to privileged access in under three hours is not going to wait for your change window. Defenders are getting faster too. We are seeing customers fix critical vulnerabilities in a median of 7 days, down from 9 last year, even as volumes rise. More to fix and less time taken to fix it tells you teams are treating this as urgent, and a count alone would never show that. We also see 12% to 16% of our customers fix vulnerabilities before the Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) adds them to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities catalog. They are acting on their threat-risk signals rather than waiting for the government to tell them. Our Threat Research Unit’s five-year analysis covered more than 1.5 billion critical vulnerability instances, and approximately 173 million of them were remediated before the vulnerability entered that catalog. Seven days is real progress, and it is still 168 hours against an attacker who needs three. The speed is not even across the environment, either. It shows up where the fix arrives on its own and deployment can be done automatically, and the network edge is still where it lags. The edge is also where a tool like ARTEX starts. So the patch window measured in weeks is finished, and policy should say so. If a fix can be deployed automatically, it goes on the same day, and people approve the exceptions instead of the rule. An internet-facing system that cannot be patched within hours gets a mitigation or comes off the internet until it can. Every risk exception signed because exploitation was hard, needed prior access, or seemed unlikely gets reopened, because in risk-register terms the impact column is where it was and the likelihood column has moved. Break The Chain at Machine Speed In ARTEX’s source, the pause between one step landing and the next step being assigned is a constant set to 800 milliseconds. That is the cadence your change window is racing. The design that makes ARTEX fast also gives you something to aim at. It works in order, and each step depends on what the previous one produced, so removing one link stops everything behind it on that route. Its planner is instructed to put depth ahead of coverage, which means it pushes a promising route all the way through instead of testing everything lightly. To a tool built that way, two medium findings on the same route are worth more than a critical on a server that leads nowhere, and a queue sorted by severity alone will keep fixing the wrong one first. The defense is to reach the link before the agent does. A program that scans on a schedule and patches on a calendar is working by the week against an attacker working by the hour, so three things have to happen without waiting for a person. The first is finding the exposure, and that has gone from weeks to minutes. Qualys InstaScan detects newly disclosed vulnerabilities on customer systems a median of 14 minutes after disclosure, with 96% detection coverage across supported vendors. Where we can compare head to head, it finds the exposure about a day before a scheduled scan would, and for a quarter of them, close to a week earlier. As AI shortens the time from disclosure to exploit, every hour of early warning counts. The second is knowing which exposures are real. Across approximately 9 million exploit validations through Qualys TruConfirm , just 11% confirmed exploitability. That turns a queue of 9 million into a queue of about 1 million, and it puts proof where a severity score used to be. Validate again after the fix, because an installed patch does not prove the route is closed. The third is fixing them without a person in the loop. Over the last 12 months, our customers deployed more than 180 million patches with Qualys Patch Management . Since frontier AI models like Mythos arrived in mid-2026, our customers have been patching 47% more each month, and the share of patches running fully automated has doubled, from about 30% last September to about 60% this September. The usual objection to automatic patching is that it breaks things. Fewer than 1 in 8,000 patches deployed through Qualys needed a rollback, and that reliability is what lets customers move at machine speed. It also frees people for the network edge, where the fix still needs hands. Not every link is a missing patch. The second step in ARTEX’s own example is credentials, and a reused admin password, an over-privileged service account, or an access key left in a public code repository will carry an attacker further than most Common Vulnerabilities and Exposures (CVEs). Put those in the program too, with owners and deadlines. What We Would Do This Week: List every internet-facing system with an open critical vulnerability or a known, exploited vulnerability, then fix it, apply mitigations, or take it offline. Search your environment for these tools, including the tomicdd/artex and congdonglinux/artex container images. Rotate any secret that was ever committed to a public repository. Deleting it from the repository is not enough. This Quarter: Move from scheduled scans to detection at disclosure wherever it is supported. Make automatic patching the default, and set the deadline for internet-facing systems in hours. Rank what is left by confirmed exploitability. Reopen the risk acceptances that were justified by attacker effort. Put credentials and exposed secrets into the vulnerability program, with owners and deadlines. Set a policy on who may run AI pentest tools, including suppliers. If you report one number upward, make it how long weaknesses on internet-facing systems stay open, because that is the number these tools are racing against. Attackers now measure time in hours. items.title: NoisyTCP: 11-Year-Old Linux Kernel Flaw Lets Unauthenticated Attackers Crash Servers Remotely
items.summary: NoisyTCP is an 11-year-old Linux kernel bug . It lets a remote attacker crash a server without logging in. The flaw is tracked as CVE-2026-99288. Hyunwoo Kim (@v4bel) reported and patched it, and he released the NoisyTCP advisory on GitHub after the Linux distribution embargo ended. The flaw sits in the kernel’s TCP code, which handles almost all network traffic on Linux. Kim says it can be triggered against plain TCP listeners. A server doesn’t need unusual settings, firewall rules, or special sockets. It only has to call listen() and receive packets from the attacker. That puts Nginx, Apache, and SSH servers in their default setups at risk, as well as proxies. The attacker needs a server with two or more receive queues, or one with Receive Packet Steering (RPS) turned on. Both are common on modern hardware. The attacker sends IPv4 fragments and normal TCP packets that land on different CPUs. This creates a race condition, where two parts of the kernel touch the same memory at the same moment. NoisyTCP Linux Kernel Flaw In the first trigger path, one CPU finds an existing half-open connection record. Another CPU frees that record and quickly reuses the same memory for a new SYN cookie request with the same connection details. The first CPU grabs the new object and passes its checks. But the new object has no listener attached. The kernel then reads a NULL listener and panics. The result is a remote denial of service. Kim warns that a crash from a containerized web server takes down the whole host, not only the app. A second path could cause a remote use-after-free, but it needs several races to succeed in a row and is much harder to pull off. Timing matters here. On virtual machines such as QEMU/KVM, the tests took about 5 seconds to 2 minutes. On a quiet bare-metal server with 8 receive queues, the tuned proof-of-concept needed about 14 hours. Cloud and virtualized servers are therefore the most exposed. This is not a remote code execution bug, at least for now. Kim says he has only built a limited, lab-specific exploit for VM servers and is still researching a general one. A reliable crash is still serious for any internet-facing service. The bug was introduced in commit 079096f103fa on October 3, 2015. The fix, commit 4e2b3ef19e0e, landed on November 3, 2026. That means nearly every Linux distribution has carried the flaw for about 11 years. Administrators should install updated kernels from their vendors as soon as they are available and reboot. If patching must wait, Kim suggests two stopgaps. The first is to turn off SYN cookies with sudo sysctl -w net.ipv4.tcp_syncookies=0. This setting applies per network namespace, so each container with its own namespace needs it too. It also weakens protection against SYN floods, a common way to knock servers offline. The second is to cut the network interface down to one receive queue and disable RPS and RFS, which stops the race. Linux networking code has had a rough few weeks. Cyber Security News recently covered attackers scanning for the Linux kernel flaw CVE-2026-98432 , a critical TCP/IPv4 bug with a 9.8 score. It also reported on a Linux kernel TCP flaw that sat hidden for seven years . Race conditions like these are hard to spot in code review, and they often stay hidden for years. Teams that run public Linux servers should check kernel versions now, test vendor patches, and watch for unexplained reboots. For background on the SYN cookie feature involved, see this LWN.net explainer. Give your SOC the alert context on the latest threats to stop incidents quickly -> Integrate Threat Intel from 16K SOCs

items.title: AWS Restores Services in US-EAST-1 After Hours-Long Outage Disrupts Cloud Operations
items.summary: Amazon Web Services restored operations in its US-EAST-1 region on November 15 after an outage disrupted account signups, authentication, and network connections. Problems began at 3:05 a.m. PST, and the last network issue was resolved at 6:21 a.m. PST, leaving some customers affected for more than three hours. The disruption affected customers using IAM Identity Center to access the AWS Console and services including Kiro and Amazon Connect. AWS also reported failed sign-up requests. Its initial service notice confirmed that engineers were investigating connectivity issues alongside problems with account access and new registrations. Service Update: Multiple Services US-EAST-1 Region We are investigating reports of Connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region. IAM Identity center sign-in requests and AWS SignUps are also impacted at this time. Track status: https://t.co/pKjXtyzPPm #AWS #AWSSupport — AWS Support (@AWSSupport) November 15, 2026 Authentication Restored Before Network Recovery AWS engineers were automatically engaged at 3:10 a.m. PST, five minutes after the incident began. Teams investigated the cause while working to restore service. Authentication issues were fully resolved by 5:20 a.m. PST, when most affected AWS services also returned to normal operation, according to the company’s update. However, network recovery took longer for a subset of customers using Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, within a single cell. Those customers continued to experience connectivity problems until 6:21 a.m. PST. The separate recovery times show why successful authentication alone did not mean every affected service connection had recovered. In its final recovery statement, AWS listed the main disruption window as 3:05 a.m. to 6:10 a.m. PST while separately confirming the final NLB fix at 6:21 a.m. PST. The company advised customers to retry failed requests and said all AWS services were operating normally. Multiple Services US-EAST-1 Region Issue Resolved Between 3:05 AM and 6:10 AM PST we experienced signup errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region. Customers using IAM Identity Center for authentication into the AWS Console, or for… — AWS Support (@AWSSupport) November 15, 2026 Previous Cloud Outages The incident follows earlier problems in the same region. Cyber Security News previously covered AWS US-EAST-1 delays affecting EC2 deployments , which also disrupted related container services in October 2025. That event provides historical context, but available evidence does not establish a shared cause with the latest outage. The disruption also came after a major Microsoft 365 outage affected Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender XDR. Microsoft reported unavailable servers, failed health checks, and capacity problems during recovery. The separate incidents highlight how failures in shared cloud systems can interrupt access to several business and security services at once. AWS’s recovery statement did not disclose a detailed root cause or identify a cyberattack. Its findings described authentication and connectivity failures. Until further technical details emerge, the incident should be treated as a service availability event rather than evidence of malicious activity or a confirmed security breach. Amazon Web Services restored operations in its US-EAST-1 region on November 15 after an outage disrupted account signups, authentication, and network connections. Problems began at 3:05 a.m. PST, and the last network issue was resolved at 6:21 a.m. PST, leaving some customers affected for more than three hours.

The disruption affected customers using IAM Identity Center to access the AWS Console and services including Kiro and Amazon Connect. AWS also reported failed sign-up requests. Its initial service notice confirmed that engineers were investigating connectivity issues alongside problems with account access and new registrations.

Service Update: Multiple Services US-EAST-1 Region

We are investigating reports of Connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region. IAM Identity center sign-in requests and AWS SignUps are also impacted at this time.

Track status: https://t.co/pKjXtyzPPm#AWS #AWSSupport

— AWS Support (@AWSSupport) November 15, 2026
Authentication Restored Before Network Recovery

AWS engineers were automatically engaged at 3:10 a.m. PST, five minutes after the incident began. Teams investigated the cause while working to restore service. Authentication issues were fully resolved by 5:20 a.m. PST, when most affected AWS services also returned to normal operation, according to the company’s update.

However, network recovery took longer for a subset of customers using Network Load Balancers, or NLBs, within a single cell. Those customers continued to experience connectivity problems until 6:21 a.m. PST. The separate recovery times show why successful authentication alone did not mean every affected service connection had recovered.

In its final recovery statement, AWS listed the main disruption window as 3:05 a.m. to 6:10 a.m. PST while separately confirming the final NLB fix at 6:21 a.m. PST. The company advised customers to retry failed requests and said all AWS services were operating normally.

Multiple Services US-EAST-1 Region Issue Resolved

Between 3:05 AM and 6:10 AM PST we experienced signup errors, authentication issues, and connectivity issues in the US-EAST-1 Region. Customers using IAM Identity Center for authentication into the AWS Console, or for…

— AWS Support (@AWSSupport) November 15, 2026
Previous Cloud Outages

The incident follows earlier problems in the same region. Cyber Security News previously covered AWS US-EAST-1 delays affecting EC2 deployments, which also disrupted related container services in October 2025. That event provides historical context, but available evidence does not establish a shared cause with the latest outage.

The disruption also came after a major Microsoft 365 outage affected Exchange Online, Teams, SharePoint, Copilot, and Defender XDR. Microsoft reported unavailable servers, failed health checks, and capacity problems during recovery. The separate incidents highlight how failures in shared cloud systems can interrupt access to several business and security services at once.

AWS’s recovery statement did not disclose a detailed root cause or identify a cyberattack. Its findings described authentication and connectivity failures. Until further technical details emerge, the incident should be treated as a service availability event rather than evidence of malicious activity or a confirmed security breach.

items.title: Tor Releases Emergency Security Update as Ongoing DDoS Attack Overwhelms Network Relays
items.summary: The Tor Project has released Tor 0.4.9.17 in an urgent response to an ongoing distributed denial-of-service attack that is overwhelming network relays. Announced on November 13, 2026, the stable release includes several security fixes, including one that addresses IPv6 handling in relay denial-of-service defenses. Tor says the attack has affected most relay operators and urges them to upgrade immediately. The attack involves a massive flood of client circuits, according to a release announcement from Tor Network Team developer David Goulet. These circuits are the connections handled across Tor’s relay network. By flooding relays with circuit activity, the attackers are placing heavy demand on the systems that carry user traffic. Tor has not published traffic volumes or identified those responsible in the announcement. IPv6 Fix Strengthens Relay Defenses The most important disclosed change concerns how relay DoS defenses handle IPv6. However, Tor’s public announcement does not explain the underlying code error, provide a CVE number, or describe the exact conditions needed to trigger it. The confirmed finding is narrower: the developers consider this fix especially important to relay protection during the current attack. That distinction matters because a security update does not automatically mean the wider attack has ended. Tor says its developers are still testing additional defenses and expect more releases soon. Version 0.4.9.17 should therefore be understood as an immediate response to an active problem, rather than a confirmed end to the disruption across the network. Tor has previously added other defenses against denial-of-service activity. Cyber Security News covered its proof-of-work protection for onion services , which makes clients complete a small computing task before their requests receive service. That earlier feature addresses onion-service access and should not be confused with the IPv6-related relay fix announced in this release. Relay Operators Urged to Update In the official security announcement , Goulet gave operators a direct instruction: “If you run a relay, please upgrade as soon as possible.” The project states that no further action is required after upgrading. It does not ask operators to apply extra configuration changes or manually adjust IPv6 settings as part of this release. The urgency reflects Tor’s reliance on volunteer-run infrastructure. Its relay operations guidance explains that volunteers provide the bandwidth supporting bridges, guards, middle relays, and exit relays. When many operators face the same circuit flood, the problem reaches beyond one server and becomes a shared network availability issue. This release targets Tor’s core relay software, not a newly announced Tor Browser build. Readers should distinguish it from browser updates, such as the previously reported Tor Browser security releases , which also address Firefox-based browser components. The immediate upgrade instruction in this announcement is specifically directed at relay operators. Tor also thanked operators sharing information through the tor-relays mailing list. Their continued reports are helping developers respond while the attack remains active. For now, the confirmed response is to install 0.4.9.17 promptly and follow further official release announcements as additional defenses become available. items.title: Claude Cracks 32-Year-Old Jeep ECU Using a $3 Arduino and Reverse Engineers Its Engine Computer

items.summary_html:
A car owner says an AI coding agent helped him read, copy, and then run code inside the engine computer of a 1994 Jeep Cherokee. The work took about a week. He used a $3 Arduino Nano, and the Jeep passed California’s smog test at the end. Muhammad Zulali shared the full story in a YouTube video on November 10, 2026.

The Jeep had no modern OBD2 port, so common scan tools could not talk to it. It failed the smog test at 25 mph because of high NOx, a gas that rises when an engine runs lean. Zulali first swapped the oxygen sensor, but the result got worse at 15 mph. Each test cost about $100, so he asked Claude Code to find a better way.

Claude found that the engine computer speaks an old, slow Chrysler protocol called SCI. The signal wire is flipped compared with a normal serial port, so a small translator was needed. A $3 Arduino Nano on a breadboard did the job, and the full parts list came to about $15.

Claude Cracks 32-Year-Old Jeep ECU

Tom’s Hardware reported that the link ran at about 7,800 baud. Only three wires from the six-hole diagnostic plug were used. One hole carries 12 volts with the key on, and touching it can fry the board.

The first reading came at 1:30 a.m. and showed only coolant temperature and battery voltage. Later data looked odd, with a fuel trim that seemed to add 22 percent extra fuel. Zulali tested fuel pressure and found a very low 10 PSI.

Claude then switched the fuel pump on by itself for about 10 seconds. He called this the moment the tool went from read-only to controlling the car.

The AI also made a mistake, and the cause was a public tool. Claude later found that the ChryslerScanner parameter table was wrong for his Jeep. The computer was removing fuel, not adding it. The scanner’s author, László Dániel, is credited in the project for the parameter tables.

Next, Claude copied the engine computer’s whole program to a laptop. The code showed a California-only fuel table that cuts fuel at the same load used in the smog test. This likely explained the high NOx. Reflashing the chip was the obvious fix, but the computer was built in December 1993, about four months too early to be reflashable.

That is where OpenAI’s Codex stepped in. It found a way to send a tiny program over the same three wires and have the computer run it. The first version was wiped out within seconds, so Codex moved the code into EEPROM, a memory that survives a dead battery. Zulali said Claude did most of the diagnosis and Codex did the memory work, while he handled wiring and driving.

The project is open source under the GPLv3 license. The xj-scanner repository on GitHub had 252 stars and 30 forks at the time of writing. It was tested on one car, a 1994 Cherokee XJ with a 4.0L engine, and the author warns that use is at your own risk.

For security readers, the lesson is about how fast AI agents can learn forgotten systems. Researchers once showed that car computers could be pushed to turn off brakes through physical access. Agents now cut the skill and time needed for that kind of work.

Our earlier report on Claude Code finding a hidden model backdoor shows the same pattern. Agents also carry their own risk, as seen when hackers hijacked Codex and Claude Code with files in Downloads. Anthropic’s Claude Code security guide advises users to review commands before approval.

Zulali admits he is not a mechanic and that some of his engine claims may be wrong. The owner reported the result himself, so it has not been independently tested.
